summary: Researchers at the University of New Hampshire say a previously unknown, very small bacterium may be behind a mysterious respiratory illness affecting dogs across the US, though the cause is not yet confirmed. The illness causes a long-lasting cough, sneezing and runny eyes, and in rare cases progresses rapidly to pneumonia and death. Experts advise owners to vaccinate pets, see a vet promptly, and avoid kennels, daycare and other crowded places.
one_line: UNH researchers identify a possible new, tiny bacterium behind the mysterious canine respiratory illness, while experts advise owners on prevention and care.
key_facts: UNH's Veterinary Diagnosis Laboratory and the Hubbard Center for Genome Studies sequenced samples from 30 New Hampshire dogs infected last year and 40 dogs from Rhode Island and Massachusetts sick this year, and found a previously unknown germ.
Dr. David Needle called the pathogen "a funky bacterium" that is smaller than a normal bacterium in both size and genome size, making it tough to find and sequence.

Graduate student Lawrence Gordon found that 21 of the initial 30 New Hampshire samples had genetic material from one atypical bacterial species after initial sequencing showed no known viral, bacterial or fungal pathogens.
The UNH team is sharing results before publishing a research article; scientists are not sure whether the same bug is sickening dogs nationwide.
Needle's team has not been able to grow the bacterium in the lab, but its structure suggests the antibiotic doxycycline may be effective.
The USDA's APHIS says it has not definitively identified the cause, and there are no reports of human illness tied to these cases.
The Oregon Agriculture Department has received more than 200 case reports from veterinarians since the beginning of August, with a very small percentage of dogs dying.

Oregon officials say the illness develops as tracheal-bronchial inflammation, chronic pneumonia, or acute pneumonia that can become severe and lead to death in as little as 24 to 36 hours; the first two respond minimally or not at all to antibiotics.

No test exists yet and symptoms resemble canine influenza and Bordetella (kennel cough), so the true case count is unknown; with hundreds of cases identified by symptoms in Oregon alone, it is likely there are thousands nationally.
Cornell virologist Colin Parrish says a viral cause is very unlikely because sequencing methods would have shown a viral signature within a few days.
Dr. Jerry Klein advises keeping dogs fully vaccinated and boosted, requesting a full respiratory panel from the vet, and avoiding grooming establishments and daycare if cases are rising locally.
Experts recommend keeping dogs out of kennels and dog parks over the holidays, with house sitters or dog walkers as alternatives.
